So I checked. Randy Gardner. Two hundred sixty-four hours. By day ten, he beat the researcher at pinball.

queue.description:
Bullfighters wave a red cape. But bulls cannot see red the way we do.

beats: [dramatic] Bulls charge red capes. But bulls cannot see red. So why do they charge?
So I checked. Cattle have only two color cones. Blue and yellow-green. To a bull, red looks dull.
I waved a red cape. Nothing. Then I waved it fast. [gasp] Now he cares.
It is the movement. Fighting bulls are bred to charge anything that moves. Even other colors work.
[dramatic] Verdict: myth. Movement, not color.
caveats: Secondary sources only (Riol et al. 'Color Perception in Fighting Cattle' not read) - phrase as 'scientists say'
'Red hides blood' is a tradition explanation - say 'it also hides blood', not as proven reason
Bullfighting is cruelty-sensitive: no gore, no harm shown, Stu is chased cartoonishly
Fighting bulls are a bred aggressive line - do not generalise to all cattle temperament

jokes.text: "Then I waved it fast. Now he cares." (red cape idle -> fast wave -> bull charges, Stu recoils)

queue.claim: Cattle are dichromats (cones near 445 nm blue and 555 nm yellow-green), red-green colorblind; a muleta is not vivid to them. The bull charges the cape's movement; the bigger capote works too; a 2007 MythBusters test found color made no difference, movement did. Cape is red by tradition and to hide blood.

queue.title: Cold Water Shock: Can You Survive 60 Seconds?
queue.description:
Falling into icy water is most dangerous in the first minute. Not from freezing. From what your body does first.

Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_shock_response, https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/medical-did-you-know/professor-popsicles-physiological-proof

Cold water is dangerous. Always wear a life jacket near water.

beats: [dramatic] Icy water is deadliest in the first minute. And not from the cold. Why?
So I checked. You gasp. Then you breathe up to ten times faster. Holding your breath drops to a few seconds.
I jumped in. [gasp] I did exactly that. Then I floated. And waited.
After about a minute, it passes. Cold takes your arms in about ten minutes. Hypothermia, about an hour.
[dramatic] Verdict: survivable. Float first. Swim later.

queue.claim: Gordon Giesbrecht's 1-10-1: about 1 min cold shock (sudden gasp, then breathing up to 6-10x normal; breath-hold drops from 60-90 s to a few seconds below ~15 C), ~10 min before arms and legs fail (3-7 min in near-freezing water), ~1 h before unconsciousness from hypothermia. Drowning mostly comes from the first two phases, not from hypothermia.

queue.title: Can You Survive a Room Hot Enough to Cook a Steak?
queue.description:
In 1775 a scientist stood in a room hotter than 260 F (127 C), where a steak cooked. He lasted eight minutes.

Sources: Blagden, Philosophical Transactions 1775 (https://archive.org/details/philtrans02639423)

Do not try this at home.

#shorts #science

New test every week on Stu Tests.
queue.approved_note: gate PASS (qa 16/0/0, fresh) 2026-11-09; kontakt-varaq ko'rildi; Blagden 1775 faktlari bank.json caveats bilan (260F bir seans; 8 daqiqa)
beats: [dramatic] A steak cooked in this room. A scientist stood inside it. How?
So I checked. Charles Blagden, seventeen seventy-five. Two hundred sixty degrees Fahrenheit. Water boils at two hundred twelve.
I tried it. Steak on a tin tray. Me beside it. [gasp] I started to sweat.
So why did he not cook? Sweat evaporates and takes the heat away. But after eight minutes, his chest tightened.
[dramatic] Verdict: survivable. For eight minutes.
caveats: 260 F was ONE session (3 Apr 1775); Banks/Solander/Phipps were in the January session at ~198-211 F (about 92-99 C), NOT 260 - do not attribute 260 to them
Steak took 13-47 min, he stayed 8 min - say 'a steak in the same room cooked', never that it cooked while he stood there for eight minutes

He was shielded: wool stockings, gloves, cloth against the red-hot stove; metal (watch chains) was too hot to touch. Stayed in the coolest spot. After 7 min breathing got tight - he left. Verdict = survivable for minutes, NOT unlimited
Dog trial: primary paper says a 32 lb bitch in a basket ~32 min, thermometer ~236 F (OCR unclear); some retellings say 1 hour - OMIT the dog
Do not imply it is safe to try; modern saunas are ~80-100 C. Do not show real-person jokes (historical, fine for Stu to joke about himself only)
Popular retelling '2600 F' is an error
queue.claim: Charles Blagden, evening of 3 April 1775, heated room (Dr Fordyce's chamber, iron stove 'cockle'): thermometer 1-2 degrees above 260 F (127 C). He stayed 8 minutes, clothed (thick wool stockings, gloves, cloth between face and stove). Breathing fine for 7 minutes, then chest oppression/anxiety, so he left. Steak and eggs on a tin frame in the same room: eggs roasted hard ~20 min, steak dressed/almost dry 47 min, another overdone 33 min, third (hotter, bellows) done in 13 min. Body stayed far cooler than air; Blagden credited perspiration (and evaporation) with cooling the body. Later he and others went in shirtless many times at almost 260 F and bore it well.

beats: [dramatic] Do sinks drain the opposite way in the south? I carried one across the equator.
So I checked. Coriolis is real. It spins hurricanes. A sink is far too small.
I drained one on each side. [gasp] Same swirl. Then I stirred it backwards. It followed.
What decides the spin? The water's earlier motion, and the basin's shape.
[dramatic] Verdict: myth. Hurricanes follow it. Sinks don't.
caveats: Do NOT use the '10,000 times too weak' figure (weak source)
Coriolis is real - the verdict is about SINKS, not the effect itself
A 1969 lab experiment detected it only with extreme effort - do not say 'impossible', say 'swamped'

jokes.text: "Same swirl. Then I stirred it backwards. It followed." (Stu stirs, tornado icon follows)

queue.claim: The Coriolis effect is real and spins hurricanes (counter-clockwise north, clockwise south) but is far too weak at sink scale; drains turn both ways in both hemispheres (Library of Congress); starting motion and basin shape decide. Equator-line demos are tricks: the water spins whichever way you start it.

So I checked. Twenty-three experiments. Sugar or placebo. The result: no effect on behavior.

queue.title: Can Quicksand Really Swallow You?
queue.description:
Movies drown people in quicksand. A Nature study says it cannot even pull you under.

Sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/437635a, https://www.nature.com/articles/news050926-9

Near a shoreline, always keep an eye on the tide.

queue.approved_note: gate PASS (qa 16/0/0, fresh) 2026-11-09 (v2 animatsiya: mocap klip/ragdoll, kamera silkinishi, ikonka jon, S1 aktyorlik); kontakt-varaq ko'rildi; faktlar bank.json caveats bilan
beats: [dramatic] Movies drown people in quicksand. A study in Nature tested it. Can quicksand actually pull you under?
So I checked. Quicksand is about twice as dense as you. So you float. You sink about halfway.
I stepped in. [gasp] Stuck at the waist. Then I moved my legs in slow, small circles. [sigh] Out.
It traps because it liquefies when disturbed, then collapses around you. It holds you. It does not swallow you.
[dramatic] Verdict: myth. The tide is the danger.
caveats: Study was salt-lake quicksand (sand, clay, salt water) - say 'quicksand' but Verdict not 'safe'
Real danger: stuck near shore as the tide comes in - include as the verdict, from secondary source
'Slowly wiggle' escape tip comes from a popular-science summary - show lightly, not as instruction
Do not say 'you cannot die in quicksand'

jokes.text: "Stuck at the waist. Slow, small circles. Out." (sand rises to waist, Stu panics, calm circles, sigh)

queue.claim: Khaldoun, Eiser, Wegdam & Bonn, Nature 437, 635 (2005): quicksand cannot suck a person under; density ~2 g/mL vs human ~1 g/mL, so you sink about halfway (to roughly the waist). It traps because it liquefies when disturbed and then collapses/compacts. Slow small circles with the limbs reintroduce water and help escape (Naked Scientists summary).
